decks.title: Blood and Lymph — Part 1: Blood, its cells and clotting
goals: State the functions of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
Identify blood cells from diagrams and explain why mammalian red cells are efficient
Outline the steps from injury to clot formation

slides.heading: Circulatory System: Blood and Lymph
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what blood is made of, and how it seals a wound.

visual.alt: Flow: blood is made of plasma, about fifty-five percent, and cells and platelets, about forty-five percent

slides.narration: Blood carries food, oxygen, wastes and heat around the body. It also fights germs and seals its own leaks. In this part we look at what blood is made of, why red cells are so good at their job, and how a clot forms.

slides.heading: Composition of blood
slides.body_md: **Blood** is a fluid connective tissue: liquid **plasma** carrying **red cells, white cells and platelets**.

rows: Water (about 90%), proteins (albumin, globulins, fibrinogen, prothrombin), glucose, amino acids, salts, urea, hormones, carbon dioxide

visual.alt: Table of the parts of blood, what each contains and its main job

slides.narration: Plasma is mostly water with many things dissolved in it: food, wastes, hormones and proteins. Floating in the plasma are the red cells, the white cells and the platelets. Each has its own job.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how much plasma?
slides.body_md: An adult has about **5 litres** of blood; about **55%** of it is plasma.
bullets: Step 1: plasma = 5 × 55 ÷ 100 = **2.75 litres**.
Step 2: cells and platelets = 5 − 2.75 = **2.25 litres**.
Step 3: so a little more than half the blood is plasma.

visual.alt: Worked table: plasma two point seven five litres, cells and platelets two point two five litres, total five litres

slides.narration: Multiply the total volume by the plasma share. Five litres of blood holds about two and three quarter litres of plasma. The rest, a little under half, is cells and platelets.

slides.heading: Blood cells under the microscope
slides.body_md: A stained blood smear shows **red cells**, five kinds of **white cells**, and **platelets**.

visual.alt: Red blood cell, five kinds of white blood cell and platelets

slides.narration: Red cells are the most common. They are discs with a pale centre and no nucleus. White cells all have a nucleus, and its shape tells you the kind. Platelets are tiny fragments.

slides.heading: Red cells, white cells and platelets

visual.alt: Table comparing red cells, white cells and platelets in number, nucleus, place of formation, life and function

slides.narration: Compare the three. Red cells are millions to every cubic millimetre, live about four months and carry oxygen. White cells are far fewer and fight germs. Platelets are fragments that help blood clot.

slides.heading: Quick check: the oxygen carrier
slides.body_md: Fill in: the red, iron-containing pigment of red cells that combines with oxygen is ______.
slides.narration: It gives blood its red colour.

slides.heading: Kinds of white blood cells

rows: Rises in allergies and worm infections

visual.alt: Table of five kinds of white blood cell with their nucleus and role

slides.narration: Neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils have granules and lobed nuclei. Lymphocytes and monocytes do not. Neutrophils and monocytes eat germs. Lymphocytes make antibodies. White cells can squeeze out of capillaries to reach an infection. This is called diapedesis.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a differential count
slides.body_md: A student counts **200** white cells in a smear.
bullets: Step 1: neutrophils 124 of 200 = **62%**.
Step 2: lymphocytes 56 of 200 = **28%**.
Step 3: neutrophils are the most common, basophils the rarest.

visual.alt: Worked table: neutrophils sixty-two percent, lymphocytes twenty-eight percent, monocytes five percent, eosinophils four percent, basophils one percent

slides.narration: Divide each count by the total and multiply by a hundred. Neutrophils come out at about sixty two percent and lymphocytes at about twenty eight percent. A big change from this pattern helps a doctor spot an infection or an allergy.

slides.heading: Quick check: white cells
slides.body_md: True or false: mature white blood cells have no nucleus.
slides.narration: Which cells in the smear lacked a nucleus?

slides.heading: Why the red cell is so efficient
slides.body_md: Mammalian red cells: **no nucleus**, **no mitochondria**, **biconcave**.

slides.heading: How blood clots

nodes.label: Injury: platelets and tissue release thromboplastin

visual.alt: Flow: thromboplastin is released, prothrombin becomes thrombin with calcium, fibrinogen becomes fibrin, the fibrin mesh traps cells to form a clot

slides.narration: Clotting is a chain. Thromboplastin from platelets and damaged tissue, helped by calcium, turns prothrombin into thrombin. Thrombin turns soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads. Vitamin K is needed to make prothrombin.

slides.heading: Inside a clot
slides.body_md: **Fibrin** threads form a mesh that traps red cells and seals the wound. The fluid that oozes out later is **serum**.

slides.narration: Start at the wound and end with the threads.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Blood = plasma (about 55%) + red cells, white cells and platelets.
Red cells carry oxygen; white cells defend; platelets start clotting.
Red cells: no nucleus, no mitochondria, biconcave: efficient oxygen carriers.
Clotting: thromboplastin → thrombin → fibrin mesh.

visual.alt: Summary table of one-word jobs of plasma, red cells, white cells and platelets

slides.narration: To recap. Plasma transports, red cells carry oxygen, white cells defend and platelets start clotting. The red cell is built for one job only, and clotting is a short chain that ends in a mesh of fibrin.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write **thromboplastin → thrombin → fibrin** in the right order and mention **calcium**.
Identify white cells by the **shape of the nucleus**.
Serum = plasma **minus fibrinogen**.
For red-cell efficiency, give the **feature and its advantage** together.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Keep the clotting chain in order and mention calcium. Use the nucleus to name white cells. Remember serum has no fibrinogen. And always pair a feature of the red cell with the advantage it brings.

slides.heading: Lymph and Blood Groups
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the fluid that bathes our cells, and why blood must be matched before a transfusion.

visual.alt: Flow: plasma leaks from capillaries as tissue fluid, which drains as lymph and returns to the blood

slides.narration: Blood never touches most of your cells directly. A watery fluid leaks out of the capillaries and bathes them. Some of it returns as lymph through a second set of vessels. Later we see why a transfusion needs the right blood group.

slides.body_md: Plasma filters out at the **arterial end** of capillaries as **tissue fluid**; most returns at the **venous end**; the extra drains as **lymph**.

slides.narration: At the arterial end, pressure pushes fluid out between the cells. It carries food and oxygen to them and collects their wastes. Most of it seeps back at the venous end. The extra enters lymph capillaries, which have closed ends, and becomes lymph.

slides.heading: Plasma, tissue fluid and lymph

visual.alt: Table comparing plasma, tissue fluid and lymph

slides.narration: Tissue fluid and lymph are both plasma that has filtered out. Big proteins and red cells stay behind in the blood. Lymph picks up many lymphocytes as it passes through the lymph nodes.

slides.heading: Quick check: tissue fluid
slides.body_md: How does tissue fluid differ from plasma?
slides.narration: What cannot pass through the capillary wall?

slides.heading: The lymphatic system

rows: Closed-ended tubes that collect extra tissue fluid
Carry lymph towards the heart; valves stop backflow
Empty lymph into large veins near the heart

visual.alt: Table of the parts of the lymphatic system and what each does

slides.narration: Lymph has no pump of its own. Muscles squeeze the vessels, and valves keep the flow going one way, towards the heart. On the way, lymph nodes act as filters. If the vessels are blocked, fluid collects and the limb swells.

slides.heading: Spleen and tonsils

rows: Destroys worn-out red cells; makes lymphocytes; filters blood; stores blood
Trap and destroy germs entering through the mouth and nose

visual.alt: Table of the functions of the spleen and the tonsils

slides.narration: The spleen is called the graveyard of red cells, because worn out red cells are broken down there. It also stores blood for emergencies. The tonsils guard the throat. When they are overwhelmed by germs they swell up.

slides.heading: Quick check: the spleen
slides.body_md: True or false: the spleen stores some blood and releases it when the body loses blood.
slides.narration: Think of the spleen as a reservoir.

slides.heading: The ABO blood groups
slides.body_md: Red cells may carry **antigen A**, **antigen B**, both or neither. Plasma carries **antibodies** against the antigens a person lacks.

visual.alt: Table of the four ABO groups with their antigens and antibodies

slides.narration: Group A has antigen A and anti-B in the plasma. Group B is the reverse. Group AB has both antigens and no antibodies. Group O has no antigens and both antibodies. A person never makes antibodies against his own antigens.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: who can give to whom?
slides.body_md: Rule: the **donor's antigens** must not meet a matching **antibody** in the patient's plasma.
bullets: Step 1: list the antigens on the donor's red cells.
Step 2: list the antibodies in the patient's plasma.
Step 3: a match (A with anti-A, B with anti-B) means **agglutination**: not safe.

visual.alt: Worked table: group O can give to all groups; group AB can give only to AB; group A can give to A and AB; group B can give to B and AB

slides.narration: Use the table row by row. Group O cells have no antigens, so they can go to anyone: O is the universal donor. Group AB plasma has no antibodies, so AB can receive from anyone: AB is the universal recipient.

slides.heading: Quick check: the universal donor
slides.body_md: Which group is called the universal donor?
slides.narration: Which red cells carry no antigen at all?

slides.heading: Finding a blood group
slides.body_md: A drop of blood is mixed with **anti-A** and **anti-B** serum. **Clumping** (agglutination) shows which antigen is present.

slides.narration: Look at each row. If the blood clumps with anti-A serum, its cells carry antigen A. If it clumps with anti-B, they carry antigen B. Clumping with both means group AB, and with neither means group O.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading the slide
slides.body_md: Read each person's two drops.
bullets: Step 1: clumped with anti-A only → group **A**.
Step 2: clumped with both → group **AB**; with neither → group **O**.
Step 3: clumped with anti-B only → group **B**.

visual.alt: Worked table: P group A, Q group AB, R group O, S group B

slides.narration: Clumping with a serum means the matching antigen is present. So P is A, Q is AB, R is O and S is B. Notice that R, the group O person, could donate to all the others.

slides.heading: The Rh factor
slides.body_md: The **Rh factor** is another antigen on red cells: people are **Rh-positive** or **Rh-negative**.

nodes.label: First birth: baby's cells enter mother's blood
Next Rh-positive baby: antibodies destroy its red cells
Prevented by an anti-Rh injection after the first delivery

visual.alt: Flow: an Rh-negative mother with an Rh-positive baby forms anti-Rh antibodies after the first birth, which can destroy the red cells of the next Rh-positive baby; an injection after the first delivery prevents this

slides.narration: Most people are Rh-positive. Trouble arises when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby. After the first birth she may form anti-Rh antibodies, which can attack a later baby. An injection given soon after the first delivery prevents this.

slides.heading: Quick check: Rh transfusions
slides.body_md: True or false: an Rh-negative person can safely receive Rh-positive blood again and again.
slides.narration: What does the body make after the first exposure?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Tissue fluid filters out of capillaries; the extra drains as lymph.
Lymphatic system: returns fluid, absorbs fats, defends the body.
Spleen destroys old red cells and stores blood; tonsils trap germs.
O is the universal donor; AB is the universal recipient.
Rh-negative mother, Rh-positive baby: risk to a later baby.

visual.alt: Summary table of the groups each ABO group can receive red cells from

slides.narration: To recap. Lymph begins as tissue fluid and returns to the blood. Lymph nodes, the spleen and the tonsils help to defend the body. Blood must be matched by its antigens, and the Rh factor matters in pregnancy as well as in transfusion.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Antigens are on the **red cells**; antibodies are in the **plasma**.
Explain universal donor and recipient by **antigens** and **antibodies**.
Rh problem: **Rh-negative mother**, **Rh-positive baby**, usually the **second** pregnancy.
Lymph flows **one way** because of **valves**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Put antigens on the cells and antibodies in the plasma. Explain donor and recipient rules with them. For Rh, name the mother and the baby correctly and say it is the later baby at risk. And remember the valves in lymph vessels.

sections.heading: 1. Composition of blood
sections.body_md:
**Blood** is a fluid connective tissue: an adult has about 5–6 litres.

**Plasma** (about 55%) is a pale yellow liquid: about 90% water, with **plasma proteins** (albumin, globulins including antibodies, **fibrinogen** and **prothrombin** for clotting), digested food (glucose, amino acids), salts, **urea**, hormones and dissolved carbon dioxide. It **transports** these substances and distributes heat.

**Formed elements** (about 45%):

| | Red blood cells (erythrocytes) | White blood cells (leucocytes) | Platelets (thrombocytes) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shape | Biconcave disc | Irregular, amoeboid | Small fragments |
| Nucleus | **Absent** in mammals | **Present** | Absent |
| Number per cubic mm | About 5 million | 5000–10 000 | 2.5–4 lakh |
| Formed in | Red bone marrow | Bone marrow; lymph nodes | Bone marrow |
| Life | About 120 days | A few days | About a week |
| Function | Carry **oxygen** (as oxyhaemoglobin) and some CO₂ | **Defence** | Start **clotting** |

**Kinds of white cells**
- **Granulocytes** (lobed nucleus, granular cytoplasm): **neutrophils** (3–5 lobes; most numerous; engulf bacteria by **phagocytosis**), **eosinophils** (2 lobes; rise in allergies and worm infections), **basophils** (S-shaped nucleus; release histamine and heparin).
- **Agranulocytes**: **lymphocytes** (large round nucleus; make **antibodies**) and **monocytes** (largest; kidney-shaped nucleus; become scavenger cells).
- White cells squeeze through capillary walls by **diapedesis** to reach infected tissue.

key_terms.definition_md: The liquid part of blood, about 55% of its volume.
Engulfing and digesting of germs by white cells.
Squeezing of white cells through capillary walls.
Proteins made by lymphocytes that destroy germs or their toxins.

sections.heading: 2. Why mammalian red blood cells are efficient
sections.body_md:
| Feature | Advantage |
|---|---|
| **No nucleus** | More space for **haemoglobin**, so more oxygen per cell |
| **No mitochondria** | Respires anaerobically, so it **does not use up** the oxygen it carries |
| **Biconcave disc** | **Large surface area** for gas exchange; thin centre gives a short diffusion distance |
| **Small and flexible** | Squeezes through narrow **capillaries** |

Because they have no nucleus, red cells cannot divide or repair themselves; they live about **120 days** and are broken down in the **spleen** and liver. More red cells are made when the body needs more oxygen, for example at high altitude.

key_terms.definition_md: Iron-containing red pigment that combines with oxygen.

sections.heading: 3. Blood coagulation
sections.body_md:
When a vessel is cut, blood **clots** and seals the wound.
1. Damaged tissue and **platelets** release **thromboplastin** (thrombokinase).
2. Thromboplastin, with **calcium ions**, converts **prothrombin** into **thrombin**.
3. Thrombin converts soluble **fibrinogen** into insoluble **fibrin** threads.
4. The fibrin mesh **traps blood cells**, forming a **clot**. As the clot shrinks, **serum** (plasma without fibrinogen) oozes out.

- **Vitamin K** is needed by the liver to make prothrombin.
- Blood does not clot inside healthy vessels: the smooth lining does not release thromboplastin, and **heparin** prevents clotting.
- Blood banks add **sodium citrate**, which removes calcium ions, to stop stored blood clotting.

key_terms.definition_md: Substance from platelets and damaged tissue that starts clotting.
Insoluble protein threads that form the clot.
Plasma without fibrinogen and other clotting factors.
A natural substance that prevents clotting inside vessels.

sections.heading: 4. Tissue fluid, lymph, spleen and tonsils
sections.body_md:
**Tissue fluid.** At the arterial end of a capillary, pressure forces plasma (without red cells and most proteins) out into the spaces between cells. This **tissue fluid** supplies food and oxygen and collects wastes. Most of it re-enters the capillary at the venous end.

**Lymph.** The extra tissue fluid drains into **lymph capillaries** (closed at one end) and is now called **lymph**: colourless, with few proteins, many **lymphocytes** and no red cells.

**Lymphatic system:** lymph capillaries → **lymph vessels** (with **valves**, so flow is one way, towards the heart) → **lymph nodes** → main lymph ducts (the thoracic duct) → large veins near the heart.

**Functions:** returns tissue fluid to the blood (blockage causes swelling); **lacteals** absorb digested fats; lymph nodes **filter germs** and make lymphocytes.

- **Spleen** — the largest lymphoid organ: destroys worn-out red cells (the graveyard of red cells), makes lymphocytes, filters blood and **stores blood**.
- **Tonsils** — lymphoid tissue at the back of the throat: trap and destroy germs entering through the mouth and nose.

key_terms.definition_md: Fluid filtered from plasma that bathes the body cells.
Tissue fluid that has entered lymph vessels.
Swelling on a lymph vessel that filters germs and makes lymphocytes.
Lymph vessel in a villus that absorbs fats.

sections.heading: 5. ABO blood groups and the Rh factor
sections.body_md:
Red cells may carry **antigens** A and B; plasma carries **antibodies** against the antigens a person lacks (discovered by Karl Landsteiner).

| Group | Antigen on red cells | Antibodies in plasma | Can receive from |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | A | anti-B | A, O |
| B | B | anti-A | B, O |
| AB | A and B | none | A, B, AB, O |
| O | none | anti-A and anti-B | O |

- **Agglutination** (clumping) happens when donor antigens meet the matching antibody in the recipient's plasma.
- **O** is the **universal donor** (no antigens); **AB** is the **universal recipient** (no antibodies).

**Rh factor.** Another antigen on red cells: **Rh-positive** (most people) or **Rh-negative**. An Rh-negative person forms anti-Rh antibodies after receiving Rh-positive blood.

**Rh incompatibility in pregnancy.** An **Rh-negative mother** carrying an **Rh-positive baby** may form anti-Rh antibodies when the baby's blood mixes with hers at birth. In a **later** Rh-positive pregnancy these antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the baby's red cells (anaemia, jaundice, possible death). An **anti-Rh injection** given to the mother soon after the first delivery prevents this.

key_terms.definition_md: A substance on red cells that can trigger antibody formation.
Clumping of red cells by matching antibodies.
Group O: red cells with no A or B antigen.
An antigen on the red cells of Rh-positive people.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying white cells have no nucleus: it is mature **red** cells that lack one.
- Writing the clotting steps out of order, or forgetting **calcium** and **vitamin K**.
- Putting antibodies on the red cells: **antigens** are on the cells, **antibodies** in the plasma.
- Calling AB the universal donor: **O** is the donor, **AB** the recipient.
- Saying the **first** Rh-positive baby is at risk: it is usually a **later** one.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term (agglutination, diapedesis, serum), an odd one out **with its category**, a blood group.
- 2 marks: a feature with its advantage, two differences, a transfusion decision with a reason.
- 3 marks: the steps of clotting, the Rh problem and its prevention, or a labelled drawing of blood cells.

questions.stem_md: Which white blood cells produce antibodies?
questions.solution_md: Lymphocytes make antibodies against germs and their toxins — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a stained smear, Tara sees the largest white cell of all, with a kidney-shaped nucleus. It is a
questions.solution_md: The monocyte is the largest white cell and has a kidney- or bean-shaped nucleus — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A child with a roundworm infection and frequent allergies is likely to show a raised count of
questions.solution_md: Eosinophils increase in allergies and in infections by parasitic worms — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A blood test shows 18 000 white cells per cubic millimetre; the laboratory's normal range is 4000 to 11 000. The most likely reason is that the person

options.text_md: has just eaten a large meal
has lost blood in an accident

questions.solution_md: White cells multiply to fight invading germs, so an infection raises the count — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In an adult human, red blood cells are produced in the
questions.solution_md: After birth, red cells are made in the red bone marrow of bones such as the ribs, sternum and vertebrae — option (b).

questions.stem_md: During a bout of dengue fever, Kunal's platelet count falls sharply. The doctor watches him closely because he is at risk of

options.text_md: bleeding that does not stop easily

questions.solution_md: Platelets start clotting, so too few of them means bleeding is hard to stop — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is NOT a function of blood plasma?

options.text_md: Carrying digested food from the intestine
Carrying most of the oxygen, bound to haemoglobin

questions.solution_md: Oxygen is carried mainly by haemoglobin inside red cells; plasma carries food, wastes, hormones and carbon dioxide — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A thorn prick on Rahul's heel becomes infected, and a thick yellowish fluid collects under the skin. This fluid is made mainly of

options.text_md: red blood cells that have lost their haemoglobin
dead white blood cells, dead germs and broken tissue
lymph that has leaked from the spleen

questions.solution_md: Pus forms where neutrophils have engulfed germs and died at the site of infection — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Mature white blood cells have no nucleus.
questions.solution_md: False. White blood cells have a nucleus; it is the mature red blood cells of mammals that lack one.

questions.stem_md: The red, iron-containing pigment in red blood cells that combines with oxygen is ______.
questions.solution_md: Haemoglobin.

questions.stem_md: An adult has 5 litres of blood, of which 55 percent is plasma. What volume of plasma, in litres, does the adult have?
questions.solution_md: $5 \times \dfrac{55}{100} = 2.75$ litres of plasma.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the squeezing of white blood cells through the walls of capillaries into the surrounding tissue.

answer.model_answer_md: **Diapedesis.**

questions.solution_md: Diapedesis.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Neutrophil, Platelet, Lymphocyte, Monocyte.

answer.model_answer_md: **Platelet**; the others are **white blood cells (leucocytes)**.

questions.solution_md: Platelets are cell fragments that help clotting.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: a doctor finds a high eosinophil count in a child who has hay fever.

answer.model_answer_md: Eosinophils **increase in allergic reactions** (and in worm infections); hay fever is an **allergy**.

questions.solution_md: Eosinophils rise in allergies.

questions.stem_md: Name two substances, other than water, carried by blood plasma, and state where each is carried to.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Digested food** such as glucose and amino acids, carried from the **small intestine** to all body cells.
2. **Urea**, carried from the **liver** to the **kidneys** for removal (also hormones, carbon dioxide, plasma proteins).

questions.solution_md: Glucose to cells; urea to kidneys.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between red blood cells and white blood cells in humans.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Red cells have **no nucleus** when mature; white cells **have a nucleus**.
2. Red cells contain **haemoglobin** and carry oxygen; white cells have no haemoglobin and **defend** the body (they are also far fewer in number).

questions.solution_md: Nucleus; haemoglobin and function; number.

questions.stem_md: Draw a neat diagram to show a red blood cell, a neutrophil, a lymphocyte and some platelets as seen under a microscope. Label each.

answer.model_answer_md: A **red blood cell** as a round disc with a **pale centre** and no nucleus; a **neutrophil** with a nucleus of **three to five lobes** and fine granules; a **lymphocyte** almost filled by a **large round nucleus**; **platelets** as small fragments with no nucleus.

questions.solution_md: Four labelled components.

marking_scheme.step: Red cell without nucleus, pale centre
Neutrophil with lobed nucleus and lymphocyte with round nucleus

questions.stem_md: The absence of a nucleus in a mature mammalian red blood cell is an advantage because it

options.text_md: lets the cell make its own proteins

questions.solution_md: Without a nucleus, the space is filled with haemoglobin, so each cell carries more oxygen — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Mature mammalian red blood cells have no mitochondria. As a result they

options.text_md: do not use up the oxygen they carry, as they respire anaerobically
cannot carry any oxygen at all
release extra oxygen into the plasma
die within a few hours of forming

questions.solution_md: With no mitochondria, red cells respire anaerobically and deliver all the oxygen they carry — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The biconcave shape of a red blood cell helps it mainly by

options.text_md: giving a large surface area for taking up oxygen
making it heavier, so it flows faster
storing extra iron in the centre

questions.solution_md: A disc hollowed on both faces has a large surface for its volume and a thin centre, so oxygen diffuses in quickly — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Deepak moves from Chennai to Leh, a town about 3500 metres above sea level. After some weeks his red blood cell count has risen, because

options.text_md: the cold destroys his white cells
his platelets turn into red cells
his plasma volume falls to zero
the air there holds less oxygen, so his body makes more red cells to carry enough of it

questions.solution_md: At high altitude each breath brings in less oxygen; the bone marrow makes more red cells to compensate — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A mammalian red blood cell can carry more oxygen than it could if it had a nucleus.

**Reason (R):** The absence of a nucleus leaves more space for haemoglobin.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the extra space for haemoglobin is exactly why the cell carries more oxygen — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A red blood cell lives for about 120 days. Assuming the number of red cells stays steady, roughly what percentage of them must be replaced every day? Give the answer to two decimal places.
questions.solution_md: One-120th of the cells is replaced each day: $\dfrac{1}{120} \times 100 \approx 0.83$ percent.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: mature red blood cells in humans cannot divide.

answer.model_answer_md: They have **no nucleus**, so they cannot copy their genetic material and divide.

questions.solution_md: No nucleus.

questions.stem_md: Explain two features that make a mammalian red blood cell efficient at carrying oxygen.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It has **no nucleus**, so more of its space is filled with **haemoglobin**.
2. It is a **biconcave disc**, giving a **large surface area** and a thin centre for quick diffusion of oxygen (it also has no mitochondria, so it uses none of the oxygen).

questions.solution_md: No nucleus; biconcave shape; no mitochondria.

questions.stem_md: Which sequence of events in blood clotting is correct?

options.text_md: Fibrin formed → thrombin changed to prothrombin → thromboplastin released
Thromboplastin released → prothrombin changed to thrombin → fibrinogen changed to fibrin
Prothrombin changed to fibrinogen → thrombin released → fibrin dissolved
Fibrinogen changed to thromboplastin → fibrin changed to thrombin → clot dissolves

questions.solution_md: Thromboplastin, with calcium ions, turns prothrombin into thrombin; thrombin turns soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which vitamin does the liver need to make prothrombin?
questions.solution_md: Vitamin K is needed for the synthesis of prothrombin; its lack delays clotting — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A blood bank adds sodium citrate, which removes calcium ions, to every bag of donated blood. This

options.text_md: stops the blood from clotting in the bag
changes the blood group of the donor

questions.solution_md: Calcium ions are needed to turn prothrombin into thrombin, so without them the blood stays liquid — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Blood does not normally clot inside healthy blood vessels.

**Reason (R):** Fibrinogen is absent from the plasma of circulating blood.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true (the smooth lining releases no thromboplastin, and heparin prevents clotting). The reason is false: fibrinogen is always present in plasma — option (a).

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but where platelets come from does not explain their role, which is to release thromboplastin at a wound — option (d).

answer.model_answer_md: **Thromboplastin** (thrombokinase).

questions.solution_md: Thromboplastin.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the pale yellow fluid that oozes out as a blood clot shrinks.

answer.model_answer_md: **Serum.**

questions.solution_md: Serum.

answer.model_answer_md: **Heparin**; the others **take part in blood clotting** (heparin prevents it).

questions.solution_md: Heparin is an anticoagulant.

questions.stem_md: Outline the steps by which blood clots at a cut.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Injured tissue and **platelets** release **thromboplastin**.
2. Thromboplastin, with **calcium ions**, converts **prothrombin** into **thrombin**.
3. Thrombin converts soluble **fibrinogen** into insoluble **fibrin** threads, which form a mesh that **traps blood cells**, forming the clot.

questions.solution_md: Thromboplastin; thrombin; fibrin mesh.

questions.stem_md: Tissue fluid differs from blood plasma in that it

options.text_md: has far fewer proteins and no red blood cells

questions.solution_md: Large plasma proteins and red cells cannot leak through capillary walls, so tissue fluid lacks them — option (a).

questions.stem_md: After a meal rich in butter, most of the digested fat is absorbed in the small intestine into the

options.text_md: lacteals, the lymph vessels of the villi

questions.solution_md: Fatty acids and glycerol pass into the lacteals and reach the blood through the lymph — option (b).

options.text_md: trap germs from the lymph and make more lymphocytes

questions.solution_md: Lymph nodes filter germs out of the lymph and multiply lymphocytes, so they enlarge — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which organ is called the graveyard of red blood cells?
questions.solution_md: The spleen breaks down worn-out red blood cells — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In filariasis, worms block the lymph vessels of a leg, and the leg swells badly. This happens because

options.text_md: red blood cells collect under the skin
the arteries of the leg burst
the bones of the leg grow larger
tissue fluid cannot drain away as lymph

questions.solution_md: Excess tissue fluid normally drains into lymph vessels; when they are blocked it builds up and the leg swells — option (d).

questions.stem_md: During a long run, the flow of lymph in Gita's legs increases. The main reason is that

options.text_md: the lymph has its own heart, which beats faster during exercise
her lymph vessels change into arteries
her contracting leg muscles squeeze the lymph vessels, and valves keep the lymph moving towards the heart
her lymph nodes pump the lymph downwards

questions.solution_md: Lymph has no pump; muscle contractions squeeze the vessels and valves prevent backflow — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Lymph flows in one direction only, towards the heart.

**Reason (R):** Lymph vessels have valves.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the valves, which stop backflow, explain the one-way flow — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The spleen stores some blood and releases it into circulation when the body loses blood.
questions.solution_md: True. The spleen acts as a blood reservoir, besides breaking down old red cells and making lymphocytes.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Spleen, Tonsils, Lymph nodes, Liver.

answer.model_answer_md: **Liver**; the others are **lymphoid organs** (parts of the lymphatic system).

questions.solution_md: The liver is a digestive gland.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: lymph vessels contain many valves.

answer.model_answer_md: The valves **prevent the backflow** of lymph, so it moves **one way, towards the heart**, although there is no pump.

questions.solution_md: Prevent backflow.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between blood and lymph.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Blood contains **red blood cells** and is red; lymph has **no red cells** and is colourless or pale yellow.
2. Blood has **more proteins**; lymph has **fewer proteins** and many **lymphocytes**, and it flows only towards the heart.

questions.solution_md: Red cells; proteins; direction.

questions.stem_md: State three functions of the lymphatic system.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It **returns excess tissue fluid** to the blood, so the tissues do not swell.
2. Its **lacteals absorb digested fats** from the villi of the small intestine.
3. Its **lymph nodes** filter out germs and make **lymphocytes**, which defend the body.

questions.solution_md: Drainage; fat absorption; defence.

questions.solution_md: Group O red cells carry no A or B antigen, so the recipient's antibodies cannot clump them — option (c).

options.text_md: has both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
has neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies

options.text_md: an Rh-positive mother carries an Rh-negative baby
the mother and baby are both Rh-positive
an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby in a later pregnancy

questions.passage_md:
Anil, aged 16, has been feeling tired and breathless and has had a fever for three days. Part of his blood report is shown.

| Test | Anil | Normal range |
|---|---|---|
| Red blood cells (million per cubic mm) | 3.1 | 4.5 to 5.5 |
| Haemoglobin (g per 100 mL) | 8 | 13 to 17 |
| White blood cells (per cubic mm) | 16500 | 4000 to 11000 |
| Platelets (lakh per cubic mm) | 2.6 | 1.5 to 4.5 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **white blood cell** count.

**(b)** 1.4

**(c)** **Anaemia.** With too few red cells and too little **haemoglobin**, his blood **carries less oxygen** to the tissues, so the cells release less energy; he tires easily and breathes faster to make up.

**(d)** His fever suggests an **infection**; white cells **multiply** to fight it. **Neutrophils and monocytes engulf germs** (phagocytosis), and **lymphocytes make antibodies** that destroy germs and their toxins.

**(e)** (i) 1. **No nucleus**: more space for **haemoglobin**, so more oxygen per cell.
2. **No mitochondria**: the cell respires anaerobically and **does not use up** the oxygen it carries.
3. **Biconcave disc**: a **large surface area** and thin centre for fast diffusion, and it is flexible enough to pass through narrow capillaries.

**OR** (ii) They are made in the **red bone marrow**; worn-out cells are destroyed mainly in the **spleen** (and liver); each lives for about **120 days**.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** White cells.

**(b)** $4.5 - 3.1 = 1.4$ million per cubic mm below the lower limit.

**(c)** Anaemia; less oxygen.

**(d)** Infection; phagocytosis; antibodies.

**(e)** (i) No nucleus; no mitochondria; biconcave.

(ii) Bone marrow; spleen; 120 days.

children.stem_md: Which value in the report is above the normal range?

answer.model_answer_md: The **white blood cell** count.

children.stem_md: By how many million per cubic mm is Anil's red cell count below the lower limit of the normal range?
children.solution_md: $4.5 - 3.1 = 1.4$ million per cubic mm below the lower limit.

children.stem_md: Name the condition suggested by his red cell and haemoglobin values, and explain why it makes him tired and breathless.

answer.model_answer_md: **Anaemia.** With too few red cells and too little **haemoglobin**, his blood **carries less oxygen** to the tissues, so the cells release less energy; he tires easily and breathes faster to make up.

children.stem_md: Suggest why his white cell count is high and state two ways in which white cells protect the body.

answer.model_answer_md: His fever suggests an **infection**; white cells **multiply** to fight it. **Neutrophils and monocytes engulf germs** (phagocytosis), and **lymphocytes make antibodies** that destroy germs and their toxins.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Explain three features of a normal mammalian red blood cell that make it an efficient oxygen carrier.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **No nucleus**: more space for **haemoglobin**, so more oxygen per cell.
2. **No mitochondria**: the cell respires anaerobically and **does not use up** the oxygen it carries.
3. **Biconcave disc**: a **large surface area** and thin centre for fast diffusion, and it is flexible enough to pass through narrow capillaries.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): State where red blood cells are made in an adult like Anil, where worn-out ones are destroyed, and how long a red blood cell lives.

answer.model_answer_md: They are made in the **red bone marrow**; worn-out cells are destroyed mainly in the **spleen** (and liver); each lives for about **120 days**.

questions.stem_md: Read the following and answer the questions.
questions.passage_md:
A laboratory student counted the white blood cells in a stained blood smear and recorded the kinds she saw.

| Kind of white cell | Number counted |
|---|---|
| Neutrophils | 124 |
| Lymphocytes | 56 |
| Monocytes | 10 |
| Eosinophils | 8 |
| Basophils | 2 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 62 %

**(b)** **Basophils.**

**(c)** 28 %

**(d)** A **neutrophil** has a nucleus of **three to five lobes** joined by thin strands. A **lymphocyte** is small and almost filled by a **large round nucleus**. A **monocyte** is the **largest** white cell and has a **kidney-shaped (bean-shaped) nucleus**.

**(e)** (i) Neutrophils squeeze out of the capillaries into the wound (**diapedesis**). They move like an amoeba towards the bacteria, **surround and engulf** them (**phagocytosis**) and **digest** them with enzymes. Dead neutrophils and germs collect as **pus**.

**OR** (ii) **Eosinophils** rise in number during allergies such as hay fever and in worm infections; their nucleus has **two lobes** and the granules stain red. **Basophils** release **histamine** (and heparin); their nucleus is **S-shaped** (lobed) and is often hidden by dark granules.

children.stem_md: What percentage of the white cells counted were neutrophils?
Which kind of white cell was the least common in her count?

answer.model_answer_md: **Basophils.**

children.stem_md: What percentage of the cells counted were the cells that make antibodies?
How could she tell a neutrophil, a lymphocyte and a monocyte apart by their nuclei?

answer.model_answer_md: A **neutrophil** has a nucleus of **three to five lobes** joined by thin strands. A **lymphocyte** is small and almost filled by a **large round nucleus**. A **monocyte** is the **largest** white cell and has a **kidney-shaped (bean-shaped) nucleus**.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Neutrophils were the most common cells. Explain how they protect the body when bacteria enter a cut.

answer.model_answer_md: Neutrophils squeeze out of the capillaries into the wound (**diapedesis**). They move like an amoeba towards the bacteria, **surround and engulf** them (**phagocytosis**) and **digest** them with enzymes. Dead neutrophils and germs collect as **pus**.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Name the white cells that rise in allergies and those that release histamine, and state one feature of the nucleus of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Eosinophils** rise in number during allergies such as hay fever and in worm infections; their nucleus has **two lobes** and the granules stain red. **Basophils** release **histamine** (and heparin); their nucleus is **S-shaped** (lobed) and is often hidden by dark granules.

questions.stem_md: Read the following and answer the questions.
questions.passage_md: Meena cut her finger while chopping vegetables. Blood flowed at first, but within about five minutes a dark red clot had sealed the cut. Later a little pale yellow fluid oozed from the edge of the clot. Her grandfather, who takes tablets that slow clotting, bleeds for much longer from small cuts.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Fibrin.**

**(b)** Platelets and the damaged tissue release **thromboplastin**. With **calcium ions**, it converts **prothrombin** in the plasma into **thrombin**. Thrombin converts soluble **fibrinogen** into insoluble **fibrin** threads, which form a mesh that **traps red cells**: this is the clot.

**(c)** It is **serum**. Serum is plasma **without fibrinogen** and the other clotting factors, which were used up in the clot, so serum **cannot clot**.

**(d)** **Vitamin K.** The liver needs it to make **prothrombin**; without enough of it, too little thrombin forms and clotting is **delayed**.

**(e)** (i) The smooth lining of healthy vessels does **not damage platelets**, so **no thromboplastin** is released; the blood also carries **heparin**, which prevents clotting.

**OR** (ii) His tablets **slow clotting**, so even a small cut or a tooth extraction may **bleed for a long time**. The dentist may need to **adjust the treatment** or be ready to stop the bleeding.

questions.stem_md: Read the following and answer the questions.
questions.passage_md: Sunita had a sore throat and fever. Her doctor felt swollen, tender lumps under her jaw and in her neck and saw that two masses of tissue at the back of her throat were red and enlarged. He explained that these are part of a system of vessels that carries a colourless fluid from the tissues back to the blood.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Lymph nodes** (lymph glands).

**(b)** Lymph nodes **filter germs** out of the lymph and trap them. During an infection they make **large numbers of lymphocytes** to fight the germs, so they **enlarge** and become tender.

**(c)** They are the **tonsils**, masses of **lymphoid tissue**. They **trap and destroy germs** entering through the mouth and nose; when overwhelmed by infection they become inflamed (tonsillitis).

**(d)** At the arterial end of capillaries, plasma **filters out** (without red cells and large proteins) to form **tissue fluid**, which bathes the cells. Most returns to the capillaries; the **extra drains into lymph capillaries**, where it is called **lymph**.

**(e)** (i) 1. It **destroys worn-out red blood cells** (the graveyard of red cells).
2. It **makes lymphocytes** and filters germs from the blood.
3. It **stores blood** and releases it into circulation after heavy bleeding.

**OR** (ii) 1. Blood has **red blood cells** and is red; lymph has **none** and is colourless.
2. Blood has **more plasma proteins**; lymph has **fewer**.
3. Blood flows **both away from and back to** the heart in a closed circuit; lymph flows **only towards** the heart.

questions.passage_md: In a school health camp, drops of blood from four students, P, Q, R and S, were each mixed with anti-A serum and with anti-B serum on a glass slide. The diagram shows the results after two minutes.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **P: group A** (clumps with anti-A only); **Q: group AB** (clumps with both); **R: group O** (clumps with neither); **S: group B** (clumps with anti-B only).

**(b)** **R** (group O).

**(c)** **No.** S is group **B**, so S's red cells carry **antigen B**. P is group **A**, so P's plasma has **anti-B antibodies**, which would **clump** the donated cells.

**(d)** **Q (group AB):** **no** anti-A or anti-B antibodies. **R (group O):** **both anti-A and anti-B** antibodies.

**(e)** The patient's **antibodies** react with the **antigens** on the donated red cells and make them **clump (agglutinate)**. The clumps **block small blood vessels** and the cells burst, so tissues are starved of oxygen and the **kidneys** can be damaged; the reaction can be **fatal**.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** P A; Q AB; R O; S B.

**(b)** R.

**(c)** No.

**(d)** Q none; R both.

**(e)** Agglutination blocks vessels.

children.stem_md: Write the ABO blood group of each of the four students.

answer.model_answer_md: **P: group A** (clumps with anti-A only); **Q: group AB** (clumps with both); **R: group O** (clumps with neither); **S: group B** (clumps with anti-B only).

children.solution_md: P A; Q AB; R O; S B.

children.stem_md: Which student is a universal donor?

answer.model_answer_md: **R** (group O).

children.stem_md: Can S donate red cells to P? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: **No.** S is group **B**, so S's red cells carry **antigen B**. P is group **A**, so P's plasma has **anti-B antibodies**, which would **clump** the donated cells.

children.stem_md: Which antibodies are present in the plasma of Q and of R?

answer.model_answer_md: **Q (group AB):** **no** anti-A or anti-B antibodies. **R (group O):** **both anti-A and anti-B** antibodies.

children.stem_md: Explain why a transfusion of the wrong group of blood can be dangerous.

answer.model_answer_md: The patient's **antibodies** react with the **antigens** on the donated red cells and make them **clump (agglutinate)**. The clumps **block small blood vessels** and the cells burst, so tissues are starved of oxygen and the **kidneys** can be damaged; the reaction can be **fatal**.

questions.stem_md: Read the following and answer the questions.
questions.passage_md: Priya, who is Rh-negative, is married to Arvind, who is Rh-positive. Their first child, Rh-positive, was born healthy. Within three days of the delivery, the doctor gave Priya an injection and explained that it would protect any future Rh-positive baby. Priya's blood group is B.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A **protein (antigen)** on the surface of the **red blood cells** of Rh-positive people.

**(b)** The baby's blood **does not mix** much with Priya's during pregnancy. Priya makes **anti-Rh antibodies** only after the baby's Rh-positive cells enter her blood at **birth**, which was too late to harm this baby.

**(c)** Priya's **anti-Rh antibodies** would **cross the placenta** into the baby. They would **destroy the baby's red blood cells**, causing severe **anaemia and jaundice**; the baby could be stillborn or die soon after birth (haemolytic disease of the newborn).

**(d)** It contains **anti-Rh antibodies** that destroy the baby's Rh-positive cells in Priya's blood, so she **does not make antibodies** of her own.

**(e)** She can receive **B Rh-negative** or **O Rh-negative**. Her plasma has **anti-A**, so the donor cells must carry **no antigen A** (group B or O). She is **Rh-negative** and already sensitised, so the donor must also be **Rh-negative**.
